cards.front: What are the five types of plants based on stem characteristics? Give one example each.
cards.back: Herb (soft/green stem, small — wheat, tulsi, mint), Shrub (slightly woody, branches near base — rose, hibiscus, coffee), Tree (tall, thick woody trunk — mango, neem, teak), Creeper (weak stem along ground — pumpkin, watermelon), Climber (uses support to climb — grapevine, pea plant, money plant).
cards.memory_hook: H-S-T-C-C = Herbs Stay Tiny, Creepers Climb. (Herbs, Shrubs, Trees, Creepers, Climbers)

cards.front: Is a banana plant a herb, shrub, or tree? This surprises most people — explain the correct answer.
cards.back: Banana is a HERB — the world's tallest herb. Although it looks like a tree with a 'trunk', the banana's trunk is actually made of tightly packed leaf bases (leaf sheaths) — not woody tissue. A true tree has hard, lignified (woody) cells in its trunk. The banana stem is soft and non-woody. After fruiting, the whole plant dies — trees do not die like this.
cards.memory_hook: Banana trunk = rolled-up leaves. No wood = no tree. Tallest herb on Earth. Every exam loves this question.

cards.front: What is the difference between a creeper and a climber?
cards.back: Creeper: a plant with a very weak stem that grows (creeps) along the ground, spreading horizontally. Examples: pumpkin, watermelon, bitter gourd (when it spreads on ground). Climber: a plant with a weak stem that grows upward by using support — attaching to fences, other plants, or supports using tendrils, hooks, or by twining. Examples: grapevine, pea plant, passion fruit, cucumber (when on a trellis).
cards.memory_hook: CREEPER = CRAWLS (C-C). CLIMBER = CLIMBS UP using support. Think of a creeper spreading on the ground like a sleeping person, a climber going up like a person climbing a ladder.

cards.front: Name the parts of a leaf and describe the function of each.
cards.back: Petiole: the stalk connecting the leaf to the stem. Lamina (blade): the flat, green part where photosynthesis occurs. Midrib: the thick central vein giving structural support and conducting water/food. Veins: smaller branches from the midrib conducting water/nutrients and supporting leaf structure. Leaf base: point where petiole attaches to stem.
cards.memory_hook: PLMV = Petiole, Lamina, Midrib, Veins. 'Plants Let Most Veins supply them' — Petiole holds, Lamina works, Midrib leads, Veins branch.

cards.front: What is venation? What are the two types? Give two examples of each.
cards.back: Venation is the arrangement/pattern of veins in a leaf. Reticulate venation: veins form a net-like (reticulated) branching pattern. Examples: mango, rose, hibiscus, bean, neem. Parallel venation: veins run parallel to each other along the leaf. Examples: grass, maize, banana, rice, sugarcane.
cards.memory_hook: RE-ticulate = RE-sembles a NET (reticulate sounds like 'reticulated python' — a net-patterned snake). PARALLEL = PARALLEL railway tracks side by side.

cards.front: What is the relationship between venation type and root type?
cards.back: There is a reliable correlation in plants: Parallel venation (veins run parallel) → Fibrous root system (many thin roots of equal size). Reticulate venation (net-like veins) → Taproot system (one thick main root with lateral branches). This rule helps you predict root type from the leaf, or leaf venation from the root type.
cards.memory_hook: PF-RT: Parallel → Fibrous. Reticulate → Taproot. PF-RT = 'Perfect FiT for Root Type'. Parallel-Fibrous, Reticulate-Taproot.

cards.front: What is a taproot system? Give three examples of plants with taproots.
cards.back: A taproot system has ONE thick main root that grows straight down deep into the soil. Many smaller lateral (side) roots branch off from this main root. The taproot penetrates deep soil to access water. Examples: carrot (the carrot we eat IS the taproot), radish, beetroot, bean, pea, mango, neem, rose. All these plants also have reticulate venation.
cards.memory_hook: TAProot = one tap going DEEP. Like a drill bit — one main shaft goes down. TAP into deep water. Carrot = taproot made delicious by the plant.

cards.front: What is a fibrous root system? Give three examples.
cards.back: A fibrous root system has MANY thin roots of similar size growing from the base of the stem. There is NO single main root. The roots spread shallowly but widely through the soil. Examples: grass, wheat, rice, ragi (finger millet), maize, onion, banana. All these plants also have parallel venation.
cards.memory_hook: FIBrous = like FIBres — many thin strands of equal thickness. Like the roots of grass — you can see hundreds of equal little roots when you pull grass from the ground.

cards.front: What are the four main functions of roots?
cards.back: (1) Anchorage: hold the plant firmly in the soil against wind and rain. (2) Absorption: take up water and dissolved minerals from the soil. (3) Storage: some roots store food (carrot, radish, sweet potato store starch/sugar in the taproot). (4) Support: some roots give extra support (banyan tree's prop roots, which hang from branches and reach the ground).
cards.memory_hook: AASS = Anchor, Absorb, Store, Support. Roots do 4 jobs: hold, drink, save, prop.

cards.front: What are the four whorls of a flower, from outermost to innermost?
cards.back: From outermost to innermost: (1) Sepals (Calyx) — outermost, usually green, protect the bud. (2) Petals (Corolla) — colourful, attract pollinators (insects, birds). (3) Stamens (Androecium) — male reproductive parts; anther produces pollen. (4) Pistil / Carpel (Gynoecium) — female reproductive part; contains the ovary with ovules.
cards.memory_hook: Some Pretty Students Pass = Sepal, Petal, Stamen, Pistil (outside to inside). Or SPSP — outside to centre.

cards.front: What is a stamen? What are its parts and function?
cards.back: Stamen is the MALE reproductive organ of a flower. It has two parts: (1) Filament — the thin stalk that holds the anther up. (2) Anther — the tip at the top of the filament; it produces and releases pollen grains. Pollen grains carry the male genetic material needed for fertilisation. A flower usually has several stamens.
cards.memory_hook: STAMEN = MALE (S and M — Stamen, Male). Anther = the pollen factory at the top. Remember: STAMEN has an 'M' for Male.

cards.front: What is the pistil? What are its three parts and their functions?
cards.back: Pistil (also called carpel) is the FEMALE reproductive organ of a flower. It has three parts: (1) Stigma — sticky tip at the top; receives pollen during pollination. (2) Style — tube-like structure connecting stigma to ovary; pollen tube grows through it. (3) Ovary — contains ovules; after fertilisation, ovary → fruit and ovules → seeds.
cards.memory_hook: PISTIL = FEMALE. SSO = Stigma (sticky top), Style (tube), Ovary (bottom with seeds). Think: She Styles Ovaries — Stigma, Style, Ovary.

cards.front: What is the function of the petals in a flower? Why are they colourful?
cards.back: Petals are colourful and often fragrant to attract pollinators — insects (bees, butterflies), birds (sunbirds), or bats. Pollinators visit flowers for nectar and unknowingly transfer pollen from one flower to another, enabling fertilisation. The bright colour and fragrance are the flower's 'advertising' to attract the right pollinators. Without pollinators visiting flowers, many plants cannot reproduce.
cards.memory_hook: Petals = Pretty advertisement. 'Come get nectar!' is what the flower is saying with its colour. Bright = Buy (attracts pollinators who 'buy' with their pollen-transfer service).

cards.front: A hibiscus flower has a long tube of stamens fused together. Can you identify all four whorls in a hibiscus?
cards.back: In a hibiscus (dasavala/China rose): (1) Sepals: 5 green, leaf-like structures at the base of the flower (outermost). (2) Petals: 5 large, brightly coloured petals (red, pink, white, or yellow depending on variety). (3) Stamens: many stamens fused into a long characteristic tube (the staminal column unique to Malvaceae family) with anthers visible along the tube. (4) Pistil: the stigma and style protrude from the top of the staminal column.
cards.memory_hook: Hibiscus is the best teaching flower — all four whorls are large and clearly visible. Sepals (bottom), Petals (middle), Stamen tube (long), Pistil tip (top).

cards.front: How does water travel from the roots to the leaves of a plant? What part of the stem is involved?
cards.back: Water is absorbed from soil by root hairs on the roots. It travels upward through the plant via xylem vessels — specialised tubes in the stem that carry water and dissolved minerals from roots to leaves. This transport happens through a combination of root pressure (pushing from below) and transpiration pull (leaves losing water vapour, creating a pull that draws water upward). The evidence: put a white flower in coloured water; petals gradually change colour as coloured water travels up the xylem.
cards.memory_hook: XYLEM = X marks the path that goes up. Xylem carries water and minerals UPWARD. X for 'eXit to leaves'.

cards.front: A plant has leaves with parallel venation. What type of root system does it have, and what type of plant is it likely to be (herb/shrub/tree)?
cards.back: Parallel venation → fibrous root system. Plants with parallel venation and fibrous roots are typically monocot plants — these are mostly herbs (grasses, cereals like rice/wheat/maize/ragi) or a few tall plants like banana (which is a herb despite its size) and bamboo. They are usually not trees or shrubs (which tend to have reticulate venation and taproots).
cards.memory_hook: Parallel venation = fibrous roots = mostly herbs/monocots. Grass is the classic example — parallel lines in leaves, many thin fibrous roots.

cards.front: Karnataka's state tree is the Sandal tree. It grows in Mysuru, Chamrajnagar, and Kodagu. What type of plant is it, and what root system does it have?
cards.back: The Sandal tree (Santalum album) is a tree — it is tall, perennial, with a thick woody trunk and a characteristic fragrant heartwood. Like most trees, it has reticulate venation in its leaves and a taproot system. Sandal is semi-parasitic — its roots attach to the roots of neighbouring plants and absorb water and nutrients from them (a unique adaptation). Karnataka produces most of India's sandalwood.
cards.memory_hook: Sandal tree = tree = thick trunk = reticulate venation = taproot. Also unique: it's semi-parasitic — steals nutrients from neighbours' roots.

cards.front: What are the three functions of a stem? Give a specific example for each.
cards.back: (1) Support: The stem holds up the leaves, flowers, and fruits — e.g., the tall stem of a sunflower holds the large flower head upright toward sunlight. (2) Conduction (transport): Xylem carries water/minerals upward from roots; phloem carries food downward from leaves — demonstrated by the coloured water experiment with a white flower. (3) Storage: Some modified stems store food — potato tuber stores starch, sugarcane stem stores sugar, ginger rhizome stores nutrients.
cards.memory_hook: Stem does SCS = Support, Conduct, Store. Like a building's columns (support), plumbing (conduct), and basement storage (store).

cards.front: Ragi (finger millet) is Karnataka's most important food crop. What type of plant is it, and what does its root system look like?
cards.back: Ragi is a herb (cereal grain plant with a soft stem). It has parallel venation in its leaves and fibrous roots (many thin roots of similar size spreading from the base). This fibrous root system is excellent for preventing soil erosion — the roots bind soil tightly. Ragi is a monocot (one seed leaf) plant grown widely in Karnataka's Tumakuru, Kolar, and Ramanagara districts. It is harvested for its nutritious seeds (used to make ragi mudde and ragi rotti).
cards.memory_hook: Ragi = Herb + Parallel venation + Fibrous roots. The fibrous roots make ragi a great soil conservator — grown on slopes in Karnataka without causing erosion.

cards.front: Name Karnataka's state flower and state tree. What type of plants are they?
cards.back: State flower: Lotus (Nelumba nucifera) — an aquatic herb that grows in ponds and lakes. It has floating leaves with reticulate venation. The beautiful flower has many sepals, petals, stamens, and a unique flat receptacle. State tree: Sandal tree (Santalum album) — a semi-parasitic tree known for its aromatic heartwood. It is a tree with a thick trunk. Karnataka produces India's finest sandalwood, mainly from Mysuru and Chamrajnagar forests.
cards.memory_hook: Karnataka's floral identity: Lotus (state flower) = aquatic herb. Sandal (state tree) = semi-parasitic tree with fragrant wood. Both have reticulate venation.
